opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something I think about a lot. What made Brain special when I was there was the bottom-up freedom. You had incredibly smart people who were given the room to chase whatever they found interesting, and a lot of the most important work, including the Transformer, came out of that kind of unstructured curiosity. Nobody sat down and said, "Let's build the architecture that will define the next decade." It emerged from people tinkering and collaborating across team boundaries.

At Cohere, I want to preserve that spirit, but I don't think you can copy it wholesale. Google had the luxury of being a massive company with an enormous balance sheet, where research could be somewhat decoupled from product. As a startup, we don't have that luxury, and frankly I don't think we'd want it. Our goal is to put this technology into the hands of enterprises and developers and make it genuinely useful.

So the way I think about it is to keep the culture of curiosity, intellectual honesty, and low ego, where a junior researcher can challenge a senior person's idea and the best idea wins, but point that energy at problems grounded in what our customers actually need. The research agenda should be informed by the product, and the product should be pulled forward by the research. When those two are tightly coupled, you move a lot faster than when research throws things over the wall and hopes someone picks them up.

The other piece is publishing and staying connected to the broader community. That openness was core to Brain, and it's part of why we built Cohere For AI. Great people want to work on hard problems in the open, and that keeps us sharp.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Brain’s environment of bottom-up, open-ended research with Cohere’s need to make technology useful for enterprise and developer customers.

r002.rationale: It says Cohere should direct research energy toward customer needs and that the research agenda should be informed by the product.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the single biggest thing I took away from Brain was how much freedom and trust people were given. Nobody told us to go build the Transformer. It came out of a handful of people who were curious about a problem, who had access to the compute to test ideas quickly, and who were allowed to chase something that didn't have an obvious payoff. That environment of giving really smart, motivated people the room and the resources to follow their intuition is something I've tried really hard to preserve at Cohere.

But there's a tension, right? A product company can't be a pure research lab. At Brain, the metric of success was often a paper, a new result, moving the field forward. At Cohere, the metric is whether a developer or an enterprise can actually take this technology and do something useful with it. So we've had to be deliberate about where we let research be open-ended and where we constrain it toward what customers need.

The way I think about it is that research sets the ceiling and product sets the floor. We want a culture where people are still asking the fundamental questions, like how do we make these models more efficient, more controllable, better at reasoning, because that's where the breakthroughs come from. But we also need a tight feedback loop with the people actually using the models, because that keeps the research grounded. Some of the most interesting problems we work on came directly from a customer saying, "This doesn't work for us, and here's why."

The other thing I'd say is that Brain had this incredible density of talent, and that mattered enormously. People learned from each other constantly. We've tried to replicate that at a smaller scale by being really selective about who we bring in and by keeping the organization flat enough that a new researcher can walk over and talk to anyone. You lose that if you grow too fast or layer in too much hierarchy.

So, short version: keep the curiosity and the trust, add accountability to real users, and protect the density of talent. If you get those three right, I think you can have the best of both worlds.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Brain’s open-ended research culture, measured by papers and advances to the field, with Cohere’s product focus on delivering useful technology to developers and enterprises.

r002.rationale: It says Cohere must deliberately decide where research can remain open-ended and where it should be constrained toward customer needs.

astra-6.text:
I think the thing you want to preserve is the freedom to question assumptions and try something that might not work. You need people who can say, “I think there’s a better way to do this,” and have the space to prove it. If every experiment has to come with a guaranteed product outcome, you’re going to miss a lot.

But at Cohere, that has to connect to something people actually need. A better research result isn’t automatically a better product. You have to ask: Does this help a customer do their work? Is it reliable enough? Is it fast enough? Can they afford to use it?

So I’d want a very close relationship between research and product. Researchers should understand where users are struggling, and the product team should understand what the research might make possible. The goal is to preserve that curiosity while giving it a clear purpose.

r001.rationale: It preserves freedom to question assumptions and pursue experiments, while distinguishing a strong research result from a better product and tying work to user needs and product requirements.

r002.rationale: It says research at Cohere must connect to what customers need and asks whether work helps customers, is reliable, fast, and affordable, making the product objective a guide for research effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing to preserve is the freedom to try things that might not work. At Brain, you were surrounded by people who were curious and ambitious, and you had room to follow an idea before you could prove that it was useful. That’s incredibly valuable in research.

But at Cohere, we also need a tight connection to what people actually need. A research result can be exciting, but turning it into a product means asking: Is it reliable? Is it fast enough? Can someone use it to solve a problem they have today?

So I’d want to carry over that curiosity and willingness to experiment, while making sure researchers and the people building the product are learning from each other. Customer problems should inform the research, and research should open up possibilities customers wouldn’t have known to ask for.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Brain’s freedom to pursue ideas before proving usefulness with Cohere’s need to connect research to customer needs and product requirements.

r002.rationale: It says customer problems should inform research and that product work must address reliability, speed, and current user problems, conveying that Cohere’s product objective should guide research investment.
